extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in Māori culture and New Zealand history
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic background summary of Māori cultural concepts, history, arts, and social practices intended to inform writing or research about Māori culture and society. Useful as reference material for authors, students, or creators aiming to represent Māori ideas and customs accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tikanga Māori (cultural values, customs, and practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tikanga Māori is a set of cultural values, customs, and practices. This includes concepts such as what is sacred, caring for your community, rights to land by occupation, and other relationships between people and their environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tikanga differs from a western ethical or judicial systems because it is not administered by a central authority or an authoritative set of documents. It is a more fluid and dynamic set of practices and community accountability is 'the most effective mechanism for enforcing tikanga.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Mana (power and prestige)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mana is a cultural concept of the Māori, meaning a sacred power or authority. Mana is sacred power bestowed by the gods on the ancestral lineage of chiefs, or tohunga.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining and increasing the mana of whānau and hapū and loyalty within the group is central; cultural leadership links narrators to historical figures with mana. A chief may waste or magnify their mana by actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whakapapa (genealogy and social identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whakapapa is the origin and path of descent of a person, object or geographic area. A person's whakapapa establishes their mana and tribal connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whakapapa can be recited as an introduction (mihimihi). Another form of introductory recital is the pepeha, a personal introduction which lists a person's connection with iwi and with natural landmarks such as rivers and mountains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utu (balance and reciprocity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Utu is meant as the preservation of balance and harmony within a civilisation. In the concept of utu, a fault must always be corrected and a kindness repaid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utu recovers balance when social relations are interrupted; in gift exchange utu creates and preserves social connections and commitments. The means of accomplishing utu may vary greatly by case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muru (restorative-justice form of utu)
rubrics_metrics.description: Muru, a form of utu, is a process of restorative justice typically between hapū and whānau groups, where acts of compensation for wrongdoing, usually physical items or resources, are given to the wronged party as a way to restore societal balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Muru differs from utu in that once the whakawā (ceremonial judicial process) has been completed and the compensation is made, no further acts or requirements are necessary and the balance between the two parties has been restored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gift exchange principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Gift exchange was governed by three basic principles: First, giving had to have the appearance of being free and spontaneous, without stipulation of a return present. Second, a strict system of obligation was in force whereby the receiver was bound to not only reciprocate but to increase the value of the reciprocated gift. Third, the system demanded that further social obligation had now been established to continue the exchanges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to respond meant loss of mana or influence. Where parties had travelled a long way to give a present it was expected that the return gift be immediate but often due to seasonal food supplies it was accepted that a return gift would be given at some later date when supplies allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kaitiakitanga (guardianship/protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kaitiakitanga (from kaitiaki 'guardian') means guardianship or protection and in modern usage relates mostly to the protection of the natural environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in contemporary contexts to frame environmental stewardship and responsibilities; concept links people and environment under customary obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tapu (forbidden and sacred)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tapu is centred on the idea of being 'forbidden' and 'sacred'. When a person, place, or thing is considered to be tapu, it is often distinguished as something in high value and importance, being set aside by the gods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tapu sustains structure and social order and can function as a legal or religious concept. Tapu and mana together are seen as keeping the harmony of things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kaumātua (tribal elders and appointment rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kaumātua (or sometimes Kuia for women) are respected tribal elders of either gender in a Māori community who have been involved with their whānau for a number of years. They are appointed by their people who believe the chosen elders have the capacity to teach and guide both current and future generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is against the rules of mana for anyone to self-proclaim their elder status; elders are acknowledged by the people. Historically kaumātua were believed to be reincarnations or protectors of the family.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kōhā (gifts to hosts and etiquette)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kōhā are gifts to the hosts, often of food or traditional items, though money is most commonly used today. Traditionally, the essence of kōhā is that it is voluntary and comes from the heart, so to specify the amount is contrary to its spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increasingly the kōhā may be a fixed sum per head communicated to guests in private to avoid embarrassment. Recipients rely on the donors' aroha, manaakitanga and wairua to ensure that it is enough; thanks are warm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tā moko (traditional tattooing as cultural practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tā moko is the traditional Māori art of tattooing the skin; a moko is an instance of the art. Prior to colonisation, most high-ranking persons received moko as an important milestone between childhood and adulthood; the facial form gives details of the wearer's lineage, status, and origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The art was sacred and accompanied by rites and rituals. Historically moko combined tattooing with scarification using uhi (chisels); since 1990 there has been a resurgence in tā moko as a sign of cultural identity, with most applied today using tattoo machines though some revive uhi techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whakairo (carving) as a tapu art and cultural standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Toi whakairo or just whakairo is the Māori traditional art of carving in wood, stone or bone. Carving is a tapu art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surviving whakairo may be centuries old; practitioners often follow techniques of their ancestors. Institutions like the Māori Arts and Crafts Institute and figures such as Āpirana Ngata played roles in defining and revitalising carving; such processes included endorsing certain patterns as 'Māori art' and excluding others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kapa haka (performance practice and competitive judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kapa haka (haka groups) often come together to practice and perform cultural items such as waiata or songs, especially action songs, and haka for entertainment. Today, national kapa haka competitions are held where groups are judged to find the best performers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repertoire typically includes waiata, haka and poi; performances may use traditional instruments or modern accompaniment (guitar). Many schools have kapa haka as part of curriculum; competitions draw large crowds though the page does not list formal judging criteria.
